findings.description: publicly_accessible = true exposes the MySQL database to the internet, and combined with vpc_security_group_ids this makes the database reachable from outside the VPC. Databases should never be publicly accessible.
storage_encrypted = false leaves the database storage, automated backups, read replicas, and snapshots unencrypted, so anyone with access to the underlying storage can read the data.

The database password (var.password) is interpolated directly into the EC2 user_data script that writes it to /var/www/inc/dbinfo.inc. This places a static credential in instance metadata and on the instance filesystem, readable by anyone with describe/ec2 permissions and by any code execution on the host.

User data embeds the RDS endpoint, username, password, and database name in a world-readable location on the web server's filesystem, exposing the connection string to any vulnerability on the instance.

The policy grants s3:*, ec2:*, and rds:* on Resource "*", giving the EC2 instance administrative access across storage, compute, and database services. This is effectively full account access and violates least privilege.
The ingress rule allows MySQL (3306) from anywhere in the VPC CIDR block rather than restricting to the application security group, allowing any host in the VPC to reach the database.
The egress rule permits all protocols to 0.0.0.0/0, allowing the database security group to send traffic anywhere on the internet, enabling data exfiltration and command-and-control communication.
username = "admin" uses a well-known default administrative account name, making the database a target for credential-guessing attacks.

The catalog_db_sg security group has no inline ingress rules and relies on separate rule resources; if the inbound rule were removed, the default behavior for this group should be explicitly deny rather than left implicit. The group as defined provides no explicit restriction.

password = var.password passes the database password as a Terraform variable, and the lifecycle ignore_changes suggests it is managed outside rotation. Combined with the user_data exposure, the credential is not treated as confidential.
